title: Unpack Outcomes
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: The ninth Will to Learn strategy, Unpack Outcomes pushes back against students collapsing results into an oversimplified I got an A or I got a D, which Stuart argues quietly crushes Effort and Efficacy beliefs. His simplest version is a whole-class written reflection the day after any assessment. For students experiencing effortful failure, he outlines a one-on-one intervention protocol, complete with a diagnostic table of common ineffective study habits matched to specific fixes. He closes with guidance on test anxiety, including a research-backed reframe, I'm not nervous, I'm excited.
points: Stuart's simplest version of the strategy is a same-day-after-assessment written reflection, moving students past binary pass/fail thinking.

His diagnostic table for effortful failure pairs specific ineffective study habits, like passive rereading and phone-adjacent studying, with concrete fixes like 25-minute deep-work blocks and active self-quizzing.

He explicitly refuses the this student says they tried but didn't framing, redirecting teachers to examine the Five Key Beliefs systematically rather than defaulting to a character judgment like lazy.
The I'm excited reframe worked for a student named Grace because it's easier to redirect a high-arousal state toward a different label than to will oneself down to calm.
quotes: Lots of Effort and Efficacy beliefs are crushed each year because students are too quick to oversimplify outcomes into I got an A or I got a D.
Few things are as demoralizing for a human being as working hard at something, feeling confident going into the thing they've worked hard at, and then failing miserably to reach their goals.
This is a classic pitfall for students because it makes them familiar with the source material — yet they are unable to retrieve the concepts from their own mind.
Are you sure they didn't try? How do you know? If you don't have strong, evidence-based answers to those two questions, it's best to dissuade yourself from assumptions like this.
When students don't try, our conclusions must be wiser and more nuanced than, Well, this student is just lazy.
The gist is this: When you're nervous, that's a heightened state of psychological arousal, and heightened states of psychological arousal are tough to shoehorn down into calmness.
What's even more important to me is that, as she was taking the test, I caught her smiling.
